newsitem.title: PERU: Military chief says Peru stable due to Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Military chief says Peru stable due to Fujimori.

text.p: Armed forces chief Gen. Nicolas de Bari Hermoza voiced support Monday for an embattled President Alberto Fujimori, saying Peru was stable and attractive to foreign investors because of his policies.

"The president is the guarantee that our country has become stable ... that inflation has been controlled ... that there is a scenario of security for international investors," De Bari Hermoza told local television station Panamericana.
The remarks come just ahead of the president's annual State of the Nation address at 1100 local time/1200 EDT/1600 GMT today.
Fujimori finds himself mired in political crisis, following the resignations of several ministers from his cabinet and scandals over alleged abuses of power in his administration.

The president's perceived authoritarianism and close links to the security forces, which have been at the center of the scandals, have bitten hard into his approval ratings, which had stood above 50 percent before this year.

Fewer than one in five Peruvians now approve of his government, according to the latest polls. Some surveys show the electorate believes De Bari Hermoza and the country's national intelligence service chief, Vladimiro Montesinos, wield more power than Fujimori.
In its editorial Monday, the pro-government daily, Expreso, urged Fujimori to distance himself from the armed forces to improve his image as a democratic leader.
"It will be difficult for the government to develop a good record on the democratic front if there are not changes in its relation to the armed forces," Expreso said.

The current political turmoil, which has led to the largest and most violent street protests in Fujimori's seven years in office, has prompted some commentators to predict the military will try to end the crisis with a coup.

When Fujimori took office in 1990, hyperinflation had brought the economy to the brink of chaos while guerrilla wars threatened national security. The president's drastic fiscal reforms and the military's strong-arm tactics against the rebels restored the country's stability and led to solid economic growth.
But Peruvians are dissatisfied with the reforms, as they have not led to palpable decreases in joblessness or in Peru's staggering poverty.
Polls show the electorate hopes the president will use his State of the Nation address to map out a new course aimed at creating more jobs.
